https://humanevents.com/2026/08/07/ceuta.text: http://humanevents.com/2026/08/07/ceuta-says-up-to-5000-migrants-remain-including-thousands-of-children-after-78000-crossed-from-morocco-warns-crisis-not-over Ceuta says up to 5,000 migrants remain, including thousands of children, after 78,000 crossed from Morocco, warns crisis not over About 100 people died during the crossings. by: Roberto Wakerell-Cruz 08/07/2026 08/07/2026 About 100 people died during the crossings. Thousands of migrants are still in Spain's North African territory of Ceuta days after an unprecedented mass crossing from Morocco, with the enclave's leader warning the humanitarian and security situation has not returned to normal. Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament on Thursday that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in Ceuta after roughly 78,000 people arrived by sea over the course of just a few hours last week. He said nearly 75,000 have since been returned to Morocco, but the territory is still under strain. Vivas also said about 100 people died during the crossings, describing the incident as an "irreparable tragedy." Addressing lawmakers, Vivas criticized Spain's leftist government, saying he had warned Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez that the response came too late, reports the BBC. "The fact that we don't have numbers on how many are still in Ceuta shows how few resources we have to deal with this situation," Vivas said. He added that local officials had repeatedly warned of an increase in migrant crossings before the influx but those warnings were ignored. Vivas said Ceuta continues to face a humanitarian emergency and public order problems, adding that it is "basically impossible" to return unaccompanied minors because doing so requires their consent. Spain's interior minister has announced €25 million in funding to help care for migrant minors in Ceuta. However, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that volunteer organizations have registered 4,860 migrant children in the territory, roughly double official estimates. "Neighbours are taking them into their homes, but the situation is unsustainable," one volunteer told the newspaper. The Spanish government has deployed armed forces to both Ceuta and the nearby enclave of Melilla. The European Commission praised Spain's "swift response," even as the crisis has fueled criticism of Madrid and tensions among European Union countries. Italy temporarily suspended its Schengen arrangements with Spain, with support from Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended, despite Sánchez noting that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen Area. The cause of the mass crossings remains disputed. EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said criminal smuggling networks spreading online disinformation likely played a role, a view echoed by Sánchez. Moroccan officials, meanwhile, blamed a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling limiting the immediate return of migrants intercepted at sea. Moroccan media has also reported fresh calls circulating on social media encouraging another large-scale attempt to cross into Ceuta, despite government warnings that promoting illegal migration could result in prosecution. https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text: Brazil Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential race Seán Clarke and Tom Phillips Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.28 EDT Share The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. The president in Brazil is directly elected, and candidates need more than 50% of the vote to avoid a second round. Polls closed at 17.00 BRT / 21.00 BST. Live first round results ... Guardian graphic. Source: TSE Results by state How the election works Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest. According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction. Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars. Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins. Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027. One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.
